claim: The dorsal mesentery (DM) connects the gut tube to the body and directs the lengthening gut into stereotypical loops via left-right (LR) asymmetric cellular and extracellular behavior.
source: The dorsal mesentery (DM) connects the gut tube to the body and directs the lengthening gut into stereotypical loops via left-right (LR) asymmetric cellular and extracellular behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Savin et al., 2011; Mahadevan et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2021; Hecksher-Sørensen et al., 2004) and is consistent with established knowledge in the field.

claim: The LR asymmetry of the DM governs blood and lymphatic vessel formation for the digestive tract.
source: The LR asymmetry of the DM also governs blood and lymphatic vessel formation for the digestive tract, which is essential for prenatal organ development and postnatal vital functions including nutrient absorption.
evidence: This claim is supported by the context of the manuscript and references to prior work on DM asymmetry and vascular development.

claim: Setting up LR asymmetry for the entire body requires a Lefty1+ midline barrier to separate the two sides of the embryo.
source: Setting up LR asymmetry for the entire body requires a Lefty1+ midline barrier to separate the two sides of the embryo, without it, embryos have lethal or congenital LR patterning defects.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in developmental biology and is consistent with the literature on Lefty1 function.

claim: Without a Lefty1+ midline barrier, embryos have lethal or congenital LR patterning defects.
source: Setting up LR asymmetry for the entire body requires a Lefty1+ midline barrier to separate the two sides of the embryo, without it, embryos have lethal or congenital LR patterning defects.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in developmental biology regarding the consequences of Lefty1 loss.

claim: A midline structure composed of a transient double basement membrane separates the left and right halves of the embryonic chick DM during the establishment of intestinal and vascular asymmetries.
source: Here, we uncover a midline structure composed of a transient double basement membrane, which separates the left and right halves of the embryonic chick DM during the establishment of intestinal and vascular asymmetries.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript, supported by immunofluorescence data showing laminin localization (Figure 3E-H) and functional diffusion assays (Figure 6).

claim: The midline basement membrane is resistant to disruption by intercalation of Netrin4 (Ntn4).
source: Unlike other basement membranes of the DM, the midline is resistant to disruption by intercalation of Netrin4 (Ntn4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that Ntn4 overexpression disrupts coelomic epithelium basement membrane but not the midline (Figure 5).

claim: The atypical midline forms the boundary between left and right sides and functions as a barrier necessary to establish and protect organ asymmetry.
source: We propose that this atypical midline forms the boundary between left and right sides and functions as a barrier necessary to establish and protect organ asymmetry.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation based on the data presented in the manuscript, including cell segregation (Figure 2) and diffusion experiments (Figure 6).

claim: The left and right sides of the body are specified early in development, after the anterior/posterior and dorsal/ventral axes have been established.
source: The left and right sides of the body are specified early in development, after the anterior/posterior and dorsal/ventral axes have been established (McCain and McClay, 1994; Danos and Yost, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on axis specification.

claim: LR patterning relies heavily on the expression of Sonic hedgehog (Shh) upstream of Nodal on the left side, and the repression of these genes by Activin on the right side.
source: This patterning relies heavily on the expression of Sonic hedgehog (Shh) upstream of Nodal on the left side, and the repression of these genes by Activin on the right side (Levin et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on LR patterning mechanisms.

claim: The localization of SHH-producing cells to the left is accomplished by nodal flow in mouse, zebrafish, and Xenopus embryos.
source: The localization of SHH-producing cells to the left is accomplished by nodal flow (mouse [Nonaka et al., 1998; Nonaka et al., 2002], zebrafish [Essner et al., 2005]. and Xenopus [Schweickert et al., 2007] embryos)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on nodal flow in different species.

claim: The localization of SHH-producing cells to the left is accomplished by rotational cell movements around the node in chicken and pig embryos.
source: or rotational cell movements around the node (chicken and pig embryos) (Gros et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on rotational cell movements.

claim: Cell death at the embryonic midline may be a consequence of its abundant extracellular matrix (ECM).
source: as well as cell death at the embryonic midline that may be a consequence of its abundant extracellular matrix (ECM) (Maya-Ramos and Mikawa, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work suggesting a link between ECM and cell death at the midline.

claim: Establishing the vertebrate LR body axis depends on a midline barrier to separate side-specific diffusible signals.
source: Establishing the vertebrate LR body axis depends on a midline barrier to separate side-specific diffusible signals (Bisgrove et al., 2000; Yamamoto et al., 2003; Meno et al., 1996; Meno et al., 1998; Yoshioka et al., 1998; Bisgrove et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work on midline barriers in LR axis establishment.

claim: Lefty1 is expressed at the center of the embryo and prevents the diffusible, left-sided signal NODAL from crossing to the embryo's right side.
source: This is achieved with a highly specific expression pattern of an inhibitor, Lefty1, at the center of the embryo which prevents the diffusible, left-sided signal NODAL from crossing to the embryo's right side (Yamamoto et al., 2003; Meno et al., 1996; Meno et al., 1998; Yoshioka et al., 1998; Bisgrove et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work on Lefty1 function.

claim: Sixty percent of Lefty1-knockout mouse embryos die in utero and an additional 20% die before weaning, suffering from left isomerism of the lungs and positional defects of the heart and major vessels.
source: Sixty percent of Lefty1-knockout mouse embryos die in utero and an additional 20% die before weaning, suffering from left isomerism of the lungs (in other words, both lungs have left lung lobation) and positional defects of the heart and the major vessels leading into/out of it (Meno et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on Lefty1 knockout phenotypes.

claim: In laterally conjoined (dicephalus) twins, the left side of one embryo and the right side of the other are connected without the LEFTY1 barrier in between, and these twins often exhibit LR defects.
source: In laterally conjoined (dicephalus) twins which form when the two primitive streaks are parallel, the left side of one embryo and the right side of the other are connected without the LEFTY1 barrier in between. Consequently, these conjoined twins often exhibit LR defects (Levin et al., 1996; Tisler et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on conjoined twins and LR defects.

claim: Separation of left and right signals is fundamental in early development for setting up correct placement and LR asymmetric patterning of individual organs including the heart and gut.
source: This underscores that separation of left and right signals is fundamental in early development for setting up correct placement and LR asymmetric patterning of individual organs including the heart and gut (Essner et al., 2005; Bisgrove et al., 2000; Desgrange et al., 2018; Duboc et al., 2015; Desgrange et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work on LR patterning in organ development.

claim: Of all the organs with LR asymmetry, only the brain is known to harbor an organ-specific midline barrier.
source: Of all the organs with LR asymmetry, only the brain is known to harbor an organ-specific midline barrier (Cavalcante et al., 2002; Kullander et al., 2001; Brose et al., 1999; Kidd et al., 1998; Erskine et al., 2000; Neugebauer and Yost, 2014; Katori et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work on brain midline barriers.

claim: The intestine grows to about 8 m in adult humans.
source: During development, the intestine grows to great lengths (about 8 m in adult humans) (Hounnou et al., 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on intestinal length.

claim: The long intestinal tube must be looped to fit into the body cavity in a stereotypical, species-specific way.
source: and this long tube must be looped to fit into the body cavity in a stereotypical, species-specific way (Stevens and Hume, 1998; Savin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on gut looping patterns.

claim: 1 in 500 infants have congenital malrotation of the gut, which increases the risk of volvulus.
source: When the developmental program directing gut looping is perturbed, as is the case for 1 in 500 infants who have congenital malrotation of the gut, there is an increased risk of volvulus, a lethal self-strangulation of the gut that requires immediate pediatric surgical intervention (Torres and Ziegler, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on congenital malrotation.

claim: Gut looping is directed by the neighboring dorsal mesentery (DM).
source: The gut tube does not loop autonomously. Rather, gut looping is directed by the neighboring dorsal mesentery (DM) (Figure 1A), a thin mesodermal organ that connects the gut to the rest of the body and through which intestinal blood and lymphatic vessels traverse (Savin et al., 2011; Mahadevan et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2021; Hecksher-Sørensen et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The left and right sides of the DM take on different properties at the molecular, cellular, and extracellular levels which are critical to initiate asymmetric gut looping and vascular morphogenesis.
source: The left and right sides of the DM take on different properties at the molecular, cellular, and extracellular levels which are critical to initiate asymmetric gut looping and vascular morphogenesis (Mahadevan et al., 2014; Kurpios et al., 2008; Davis et al., 2008; Welsh et al., 2013; Sivakumar et al., 2018; Sanketi et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work on DM asymmetries.

claim: Gut tilting occurs at embryonic day 10.5 (E10.5) in the mouse and Hamburger-Hamilton stage 19–21 (HH19–21) in the chicken embryo.
source: Gut tilting is the symmetry-breaking event that initiates asymmetric gut looping, which occurs at embryonic day 10.5 (E10.5) in the mouse and Hamburger-Hamilton stage 19–21 (HH19–21) (Hamburger and Hamilton, 1951) in the chicken embryo (Figure 1; Davis et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Gut tilting is driven by the condensation of the ECM in the left DM and an expansion of the ECM on the right.
source: Gut tilting is driven by the condensation of the ECM in the left DM and an expansion of the ECM on the right (Figure 1B; Kurpios et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work and is illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Endothelial precursors exist on both the left and right DM prior to tilting, but as asymmetries are established the right-sided endothelial cells emigrate rather than forming vessels.
source: Although endothelial precursors exist on both the left and right DM prior to tilting, as the asymmetries are established the right-sided endothelial cells emigrate rather than forming vessels (Mahadevan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on vascular development in the DM.

claim: Only a left-sided gut artery develops further, which goes on to supply blood to a significant portion of the adult intestine.
source: Only a left-sided gut artery develops further (Figure 1B), which goes on to supply blood to a significant portion of the adult intestine (Figure 1A; Mahadevan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work and is illustrated in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: Right-sided endothelial cells emigrate dorsally and ventrally, but they cannot cross directly over to the left side.
source: Interestingly, these right-sided endothelial cells emigrate dorsally and ventrally, but they cannot cross directly over to the left side (Mahadevan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on endothelial cell migration.

claim: The inability of right-sided endothelial cells to cross to the left side might indicate the presence of a barrier against cell migration at the midline.
source: This might indicate the presence of a barrier against cell migration at the midline.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that right-sided endothelial cells do not cross to the left side.

claim: There is a sharp delineation between left and right DM in gene expression and protein localization, as well as LR asymmetric distribution of extracellular glycosaminoglycans, such as hyaluronan.
source: Instead of an LR gradient, however, there is a sharp delineation between left and right DM in gene expression and protein localization, as well as LR asymmetric distribution of extracellular glycosaminoglycans, such as hyaluronan (Mahadevan et al., 2014; Kurpios et al., 2008; Davis et al., 2008; Welsh et al., 2013; Sivakumar et al., 2018; Sanketi et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work on DM asymmetries.

claim: Perturbing even just one gene's asymmetric expression patterns in the DM leads to aberrant gut looping patterns and abnormal vascular lesions.
source: Not surprisingly, perturbing even just one gene's asymmetric expression patterns in the DM leads to aberrant gut looping patterns and abnormal vascular lesions (Mahadevan et al., 2014; Welsh et al., 2013; Sivakumar et al., 2018; Sanketi et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work on genetic perturbations in the DM.

claim: An atypical basement membrane forms a boundary between left and right cell populations and limits diffusion across the DM midline.
source: Here, we show that an atypical basement membrane forms a boundary between left and right cell populations and limits diffusion across the DM midline.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript, supported by cell segregation data (Figure 2) and diffusion experiments (Figure 6).

claim: The DM mesenchyme forms by bilateral epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and ingression of coelomic epithelium, which is derived from the splanchnic mesoderm.
source: The DM mesenchyme forms by bilateral epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and ingression of coelomic epithelium, which is derived from the splanchnic mesoderm; the left DM comes from the left coelom and the right DM arises from the right coelom (Figure 2A and B; Hecksher-Sørensen et al., 2004; Kurpios et al., 2008; Davis et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is illustrated in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The left DM comes from the left coelom and the right DM arises from the right coelom.
source: the left DM comes from the left coelom and the right DM arises from the right coelom (Figure 2A and B; Hecksher-Sørensen et al., 2004; Kurpios et al., 2008; Davis et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is illustrated in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Left and right cells meet at the middle of the DM but never cross over or mix.
source: While the left and right cells meet at the middle of the DM, they never cross over or mix (Mahadevan et al., 2014; Kurpios et al., 2008; Davis et al., 2008; Welsh et al., 2013; Sanketi et al., 2022; Welsh et al., 2015; Arraf et al., 2016; Arraf et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work and is visualized in Figure 2C-H.

claim: There is no visible histological boundary between the left and right sides of the DM at HH20 and HH21 as shown by H&E staining.
source: This striking separation occurs despite the lack of a visible histological boundary between the two sides as shown by H&E staining at HH20 and HH21, when the left is condensing and the right is expanding to drive the leftward gut tilting (Figure 2K and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by H&E staining data shown in Figure 2K and L.

claim: When cell-cell adhesion is interrupted in the left DM, the cells become more dispersed and extend filopodia over toward the right side, suggesting pathogenic cell migration.
source: In support of this, we have previously shown that when cell-cell adhesion is interrupted in the left DM, the cells become more dispersed (Kurpios et al., 2008; Welsh et al., 2013) and extend filopodia over toward the right side, suggesting pathogenic cell migration (Welsh et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on cell-cell adhesion in the DM.

claim: Lefty1 is expressed at the midline of early embryos (HH9).
source: While Lefty1 was expressed at the midline of early embryos as expected (Figure 3A)
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Lefty1 is not expressed at the midline of the DM at HH19.
source: it was not expressed at the midline of the DM at HH19 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) data showed a fibrous matrix between the notochord and endoderm where the DM will later develop.
source: Interestingly, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) data showed a fibrous matrix between the notochord and endoderm where the DM will later develop, suggesting that ECM may separate the two sides before they coalesce into the DM (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by SEM data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Basement membranes are dense ECM requiring laminin, collagen IV, nidogen, and perlecan and/or agrin.
source: Basement membranes are dense ECM requiring laminin, collagen IV, nidogen, and perlecan and/or agrin (both heparan sulfate proteoglycans) with a large variety of other components that can be integrated to create specific 'flavors' of basement membrane tuned to different barrier contexts (Yurchenco, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on basement membrane composition.

claim: At HH18, laminin IF marked an oval-shaped structure just ventral to the notochord and dorsal to the gut endoderm.
source: At HH18, when cellular DM asymmetries are first being initiated at the level of the midgut (which forms the small intestine), laminin IF marked an oval-shaped structure just ventral to the notochord and dorsal to the gut endoderm (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: No cells were seen within the midline structure at HH18 as shown by a lack of nuclear staining and empty space in SEM.
source: No cells were seen within this structure as shown by a lack of nuclear staining (Figure 3E) and empty space in SEM (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and SEM data shown in Figure 3E, 3C, 3D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: At HH19, the midline structure lengthened, forming two parallel lines connecting the endoderm and notochord.
source: As the DM elongates and asymmetries become more apparent (HH19), this midline structure lengthened, forming two parallel lines connecting the endoderm and notochord (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: At HH20, the midline was still present but began to appear fragmented.
source: One stage later (HH20), the midline was still present but began to appear fragmented (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: By HH21, the midline disappeared while laminin IF underlying the coelomic epithelium and endoderm remained intense.
source: By HH21, the asymmetries of the DM are established—the right DM has expanded, the left DM has condensed, the gut has tilted to the left, and vascular precursor cells have been driven out of the right side (Figure 1B; Mahadevan et al., 2014; Sanketi et al., 2022). Surprisingly, the midline disappeared by this stage, while laminin IF underlying the coelomic epithelium and endoderm remained intense (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3H and citations to prior work.

claim: The lengthening of the midline and its subsequent loss occurred in an anterior-to-posterior wave down the embryonic gut tube.
source: The lengthening of the midline and its subsequent loss occurred in an anterior-to-posterior wave down the embryonic gut tube (Figure 3J and K).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3J and K.

claim: Nidogen co-localizes with laminin at the midline.
source: To further characterize the nature of the ECM at the DM midline, we did IF staining for nidogen and perlecan, confirming co-localization with laminin at the midline barrier (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Perlecan co-localizes with laminin at the midline.
source: To further characterize the nature of the ECM at the DM midline, we did IF staining for nidogen and perlecan, confirming co-localization with laminin at the midline barrier (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The DM midline consists of basement membrane.
source: This further illustrates that the DM midline consists of basement membrane.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the co-localization of laminin, nidogen, and perlecan at the midline, which are foundational basement membrane components.

claim: This basement membrane structure is conserved in the squamate veiled chameleon, C. calyptratus, which exhibits a similarly transient double basement membrane at the midline of the DM from approximately the 7-somite stage to the 29-somite stage.
source: This basement membrane structure is conserved in the squamate veiled chameleon, C. calyptratus, which exhibits a similarly transient double basement membrane at the midline of the DM from approximately the 7-somite stage to the 29-somite stage (Figure 3—figure supplement 4; Diaz et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and a citation to prior work on chameleon development.

claim: Fibronectin localized to the dorsal aorta which often coincides with the most ventral part of the midline.
source: A common basement membrane constituent is fibronectin, which is best known for its role in the provisional matrix during wound healing (Clark et al., 1982). At our developmental stages of interest, fibronectin localized to the dorsal aorta which often coincides with the most ventral part of the midline (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and a citation to prior work on fibronectin.

claim: The midline is sandwiched between mesenchymal cells from the left and right DM, unbiased to either the left or the right side.
source: Although we have established the time kinetics of DM midline formation, the origin of this structure remains elusive. The midline is sandwiched between mesenchymal cells from the left and right DM, unbiased to either the left or the right side (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell labeling data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: Mesenchymal cells are not usually competent to construct an organized basement membrane.
source: Intriguingly, mesenchymal cells like these are not usually competent to construct an organized basement membrane (Yurchenco, 2011; Glentis et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on basement membrane formation.

claim: Mesenchymal cells can secrete matrix components, but the organization of these components into a basement membrane is dependent on the presence of cell surface anchors which are characteristic of tissues like polarized epithelium or endothelium, not mesenchymal cells.
source: Mesenchymal cells can secrete matrix components (Simon-Assmann et al., 1998), but the organization of these components into a basement membrane is dependent on the presence of cell surface anchors which are characteristic of tissues like polarized epithelium or endothelium, not mesenchymal cells (Glentis et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on basement membrane organization.

claim: LAMA1 is secreted by the epithelia in the developing intestine, not the mesenchyme.
source: In the case of LAMA1, it is known that this protein is secreted by the epithelia in the developing intestine, not the mesenchyme (Simon-Assmann et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on LAMA1 expression.

claim: RNA in situ hybridization for Lama1 did not show enriched expression in the mesenchyme at the DM midline.
source: Indeed, RNA in situ hybridization for Lama1 did not show enriched expression in the mesenchyme at the DM midline (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: The left coelomic epithelium was polarized at HH19 relative to its basement membrane as quantified by Golgi staining with GM130.
source: As expected, the left coelomic epithelium was polarized at HH19 relative to its basement membrane as quantified by Golgi staining with GM130 (Figure 4D and E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Welsh et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by GM130 staining data shown in Figure 4D and E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and a citation to prior work.

claim: Cells immediately to the left or right of the midline have random orientation.
source: However, GM130 staining and quantification showed that cells immediately to the left or right of the midline have random orientation (Figure 4D and E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by GM130 staining and quantification data shown in Figure 4D and E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Embryos isolated at HH19 and HH21 showed that GFP-labeled endodermal cells remain restricted to the endoderm—there were no GFP+ mesenchymal cells present in the DM.
source: Interestingly, embryos isolated at HH19 and HH21 showed that GFP-labeled cells remain restricted to the endoderm—there were no GFP+ mesenchymal cells present in the DM (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by endodermal electroporation and lineage tracing data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: The DM midline is not formed from EMT of basement membrane-carrying endodermal cells.
source: This indicates that the DM midline is not formed from EMT of basement membrane-carrying endodermal cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that GFP-labeled endodermal cells do not contribute to the DM mesenchyme.

claim: Laminin IF did not reveal a secondary midline-like structure associated with the ectopic notochord in notochord transplant experiments.
source: Laminin IF did not reveal a secondary midline-like structure associated with the ectopic notochord (Figure 4K and M) while the normal midline was unaffected (Figure 4K and M, white arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by notochord transplant and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4K and M.

claim: The notochord is not sufficient for the formation of DM midline.
source: From this, we conclude that the notochord is not sufficient for the formation of DM midline.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the notochord transplant experiments showing no ectopic midline formation.

claim: NTN4 has very high binding affinity for laminin gamma subunits, such that NTN4 can prevent the formation of new laminin networks and can also disrupt existing laminin networks.
source: NTN4 has very high binding affinity for laminin gamma subunits, such that NTN4 can prevent the formation of new laminin networks, which are the foundation upon which other basement membrane components assemble and can also disrupt existing laminin networks (Schneiders et al., 2007; Reuten et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on NTN4 function.

claim: When Ntn4 was overexpressed on either side of the DM by electroporation, the basement membrane underlying the coelomic epithelium was perturbed and the scattered laminin staining in the mesenchyme was depleted.
source: As expected, when we overexpressed Ntn4 on either side of the DM by electroporation, we perturbed the basement membrane underlying the coelomic epithelium and depleted the scattered laminin staining in the mesenchyme that results from EMT creating the DM (Figure 5B, D, and E vs. controls Figure 5A and C; Horejs, 2016; Hu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ntn4 overexpression and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B, D, and E compared to controls in Figure 5A and C, and citations to prior work.

claim: The DM midline basement membrane remained visibly intact in all embryos with lateral and bilateral Ntn4 overexpression in the DM.
source: Intriguingly, the DM midline basement membrane remained visibly intact in all embryos with lateral (Figure 5B and D) and bilateral (Figure 5E) Ntn4 overexpression in the DM.
evidence: This claim is supported by Ntn4 overexpression and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B, D, and E.

claim: Endodermal Ntn4 overexpression caused much less disruption of the endodermal or midline basement membranes when compared to its effect on coelomic epithelium basement membrane.
source: Similarly, endodermal Ntn4 overexpression caused much less disruption of the endodermal or midline basement membranes (Figure 5G vs. control Figure 5F) when compared to its effect on coelomic epithelium basement membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by endodermal Ntn4 overexpression and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5G compared to control in Figure 5F.

claim: The midline and endoderm may have basement membranes of the same 'flavor', possibly pointing to a common origin.
source: This suggests that the midline and endoderm may have basement membranes of the same 'flavor', possibly pointing to a common origin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar resistance of midline and endodermal basement membranes to NTN4 disruption.

claim: Genes including Cxcl12 and Bmp4 which encode diffusible signals are expressed asymmetrically in the DM.
source: Genes including Cxcl12 (Mahadevan et al., 2014; Sivakumar et al., 2018) and Bmp4 (Sanketi et al., 2022) which encode diffusible signals are expressed asymmetrically in the DM (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6A and B and citations to prior work.

claim: Genes encoding enzymes that are secreted into the ECM, like the HA-modifying enzyme TSG6, are expressed asymmetrically in the DM.
source: So too are genes encoding enzymes that are secreted into the ECM, like the HA-modifying enzyme TSG6 (Sivakumar et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on TSG6 expression.

claim: The expression domains of asymmetrically expressed genes have a sharp boundary at the midline, since left and right cells do not mix.
source: The expression domains of these genes have a sharp boundary at the midline, since left and right cells do not mix.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that left and right cells do not mix (Figure 2).

claim: Ectopic expression of pro-angiogenic Cxcl12 on the right side results in an aberrant vessel forming on the right.
source: We know that experimentally mixing left and right signals is detrimental to gut tilting and vascular patterning (Mahadevan et al., 2014; Kurpios et al., 2008; Davis et al., 2008; Welsh et al., 2013; Sivakumar et al., 2018; Sanketi et al., 2022)—e.g., ectopic expression of pro-angiogenic Cxcl12 on the right side results in an aberrant vessel forming on the right (Mahadevan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on Cxcl12 ectopic expression.

claim: When the CXCR4 receptor antagonist AMD3100 is introduced to the left DM, it abolishes vascular development on the left.
source: Moreover, when the CXCR4 receptor antagonist AMD3100 (MW = 502.78) is introduced to the left DM, it abolishes vascular development on the left.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on AMD3100 effects.

claim: When AMD3100 is introduced to the right DM, the left-sided vascular development remains intact.
source: However, when the same drug is introduced to the right DM, the left-sided vascular development remains intact (Mahadevan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on AMD3100 effects.

claim: When 3 kDa fluorescent dextran was injected into the right side of the DM at HH19 when the midline is intact, movement of dextran through the tissue was limited to the right side.
source: When these injections are performed at stages where the midline is intact (HH19), movement of dextran through the tissue was limited to the right side (n=4/4 embryos) (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by dextran injection and imaging data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: When the basement membrane midline appears fragmented (HH20), dextran injections produced mixed results—in some embryos, diffusion across the midline was prevented and in others the dextran was able to move into the left mesenchyme of the DM.
source: When the basement membrane midline appears fragmented (HH20), these injections produced mixed results—in some embryos (n=2/9), diffusion across the midline was prevented and in others (n=7/9) the dextran was able to move into the left mesenchyme of the DM (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by dextran injection and imaging data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: At stages where no organized basement membrane structure remains at the midline (HH23), diffusion of dextran was always permitted across the entire width of the DM.
source: Finally, at stages where no organized basement membrane structure remains at the midline (HH23), diffusion of dextran was always permitted across the entire width of the DM (n=7/7) (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by dextran injection and imaging data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The ratio of average AMD3100-BODIPY intensity in the right DM vs. the left DM was below 0.5 when the midline is intact (HH19), indicating little diffusion across the DM.
source: The ratio of average AMD3100-BODIPY intensity in the right DM vs. the left DM was below 0.5 when the midline is intact (HH19, n=4/4), indicating little diffusion across the DM (Figure 6J).
evidence: This claim is supported by AMD3100-BODIPY beading and imaging data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: When no midline remains at HH21, the ratio of AMD3100-BODIPY intensity in right vs. left DM significantly rises to near one, indicating diffusion of the drug is not impeded when the midline basement membrane structure is absent.
source: When no midline remains at a later stage (HH21, n=4/4), this ratio significantly rises to near one, indicating diffusion of the drug is not impeded when the midline basement membrane structure is absent (Figure 6J).
evidence: This claim is supported by AMD3100-BODIPY beading and imaging data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: The basement membrane structure at the midline forms a transient functional barrier against diffusion.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that the basement membrane structure at the midline forms a transient functional barrier against diffusion (Figure 6M).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the dextran and AMD3100-BODIPY diffusion experiments.

claim: The brain has the only known organ-specific midline barrier, where commissural axons of the brain and spinal cord are tightly controlled by midline-localized guidance and repulsion cues including FGFs, SLIT/ROBO signaling, EFNB3, heparan sulfate proteoglycans, and the Rac-specific GTPase-activating protein α-chimaerin.
source: Individual organs, too, have LR asymmetries, but the brain has the only known organ-specific midline barrier, where commissural axons of the brain and spinal cord are tightly controlled by midline-localized guidance and repulsion cues including FGFs, SLIT/ROBO signaling, EFNB3, heparan sulfate proteoglycans, and the Rac-specific GTPase-activating protein α-chimaerin (Cavalcante et al., 2002; Kullander et al., 2001; Brose et al., 1999; Kidd et al., 1998; Erskine et al., 2000; Neugebauer and Yost, 2014; Katori et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work on brain midline barriers.

claim: Some morphogens (like Nodal) can induce effects at distances of 200 μm or greater.
source: While the diffusion of a given signal depends on the tissue context (Müller et al., 2013). some morphogens (like Nodal) can induce effects at distances of 200 μm or greater (Müller and Schier, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on morphogen diffusion.

claim: The HH19 DM is only about 150 μm across.
source: The HH19 DM is only about 150 μm across, not a prohibitive distance for diffusible signals like BMPs, TGFβ (Sanketi et al., 2022), and CXCL12 (Mahadevan et al., 2014) to cross between the left and right DM.
evidence: This is an observation based on measurements of the DM and is used to support the hypothesis that a barrier is needed.

claim: The midline limits diffusion of dextran from right to left, which suggests that it also blocks the movement of endogenous diffusible signals.
source: In support of this, we showed that the midline limits diffusion of dextran from right to left, which suggests that it also blocks the movement of endogenous diffusible signals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dextran diffusion experiments.

claim: Dextran's inability to cross the midline indicates that diffusible proteins of typical weight (such as CXCL12 at 10 kDa and BMP4 at 34 kDa) are also unable to cross.
source: Moreover, with a molecular weight of just 3 kDa, dextran's inability to cross the midline indicates that diffusible proteins of typical weight (such as CXCL12 at 10 kDa and BMP4 at 34 kDa) are also unable to cross.
evidence: This is an inference based on the molecular weight of dextran and the diffusion experiments.

claim: Basement membranes play many critical barrier functions in the embryo and adult, usually found as a single layer that underlies polarized epithelial or endothelial cell layers.
source: Basement membranes play many critical barrier functions in the embryo and adult, usually found as a single layer that underlies polarized epithelial or endothelial cell layers such as those lining the intestines, encircling blood vessels, or enveloping muscle cells, adipocytes, or Schwann cells (Yurchenco, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on basement membrane function and is established knowledge.

claim: Null mutations in genes encoding basement membrane components often result in embryonic lethality and postnatal pathologies.
source: As such, null mutations in genes encoding basement membrane components often result in embryonic lethality and postnatal pathologies (Bader et al., 2005; Miner et al., 2004; Smyth et al., 1999; Gatseva et al., 2019; Pozzi et al., 2017; Yao, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work on basement membrane mutations.

claim: A role for basement membrane in establishing LR asymmetry has not been described previously.
source: However, a role for basement membrane in establishing LR asymmetry has not been described previously.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings in the manuscript.

claim: The basement membrane we describe here is atypical in its double membrane structure.
source: The basement membrane we describe here is atypical in its double membrane structure, which raises interesting questions about its formation.
evidence: This is a characterization of the midline basement membrane based on the data presented.

claim: Upon electroporation of the endoderm with GFP, GFP-positive cells were not detected in the DM later in development but remained restricted to the endoderm, indicating that the midline does not form from EMT of basement membrane-carrying endodermal cells.
source: Upon electroporation of the endoderm with GFP, GFP-positive cells were not detected in the DM later in development but remained restricted to the endoderm (Figure 4F–H), indicating that the midline does not form from EMT of basement membrane-carrying endodermal cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by endodermal electroporation and lineage tracing data shown in Figure 4F-H.

claim: There was no appreciable cell death observed by TUNEL staining at the midline during the stages of interest.
source: We can also eliminate endodermal death as a possible mechanism, because there was no appreciable cell death observed by TUNEL staining at the midline during the stages of interest (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on TUNEL staining data that is mentioned but not shown.

claim: The midline does not form in the same way as other double basement membranes, which arise from the meeting of the basal sides of two tissues.
source: Nor does the midline form in the same way as other double basement membranes, which arise from the meeting of the basal sides of two tissues (Keeley and Sherwood, 2019; Pastor-Pareja, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on double basement membrane formation.

claim: In the case of the DM midline barrier, the apical sides of the endodermal cells are facing each other.
source: Instead in the case of the DM midline barrier, the apical sides of the endodermal cells are facing each other.
evidence: This is an observation based on the structure of the DM and endoderm.

claim: The midline forms when basement membrane is left behind as the endoderm descends ventrally during normal development, as if it were a 'scar' of where the endoderm was previously.
source: We hypothesize that the midline forms when basement membrane is left behind as the endoderm descends ventrally during normal development, as if it were a 'scar' of where the endoderm was previously (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations and is illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: During early development the notochord is embedded within the endoderm and a basement membrane covers the two structures.
source: During early development the notochord is embedded within the endoderm and a basement membrane covers the two structures. Only later are the two structures separated by a full basement membrane, pointing to a strong connection between the two (Fausett et al., 2014; Jurand, 1974).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on notochord and endoderm development.

claim: The medial migration of the aortae and coelomic epithelia could provide tissue forces that push the notochord and endoderm apart, leaving behind basement membrane at the DM midline.
source: The medial migration of the aortae and coelomic epithelia could provide tissue forces that push the notochord and endoderm apart, leaving behind basement membrane at the DM midline.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations.

claim: The observation that the basement membranes of both the endoderm and midline were resistant to disruption by NTN4 could support the idea that the endoderm is responsible for making both basement membranes.
source: The observation that the basement membranes of both the endoderm and midline were resistant to disruption by NTN4 could also support the idea that the endoderm is responsible for making both basement membranes (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an inference based on the NTN4 overexpression experiments and is illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The basement membrane underlying the gut endoderm does not co-migrate with the intestinal epithelial cells as they move from the proliferative intestinal crypts to the tip of the villus over the course of 3–6 days in the adult; the basement membrane is instead left in place.
source: In support of this, we know that the basement membrane underlying the gut endoderm does not co-migrate with the intestinal epithelial cells as they move from the proliferative intestinal crypts to the tip of the villus over the course of 3–6 days in the adult; the basement membrane is instead left in place. (Trier et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on intestinal epithelial cell migration.

claim: The endodermal basement membrane and midline's resistance to NTN4 disruption is particularly notable, as similar resistance has not been reported before.
source: The endodermal basement membrane and midline's resistance to NTN4 disruption is particularly notable, as similar resistance has not been reported before.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings in the manuscript.

claim: The resistance of endodermal and midline basement membranes to NTN4 suggests the presence of an unknown factor or modification that shields or stabilizes the laminin network from NTN4 binding.
source: This suggests the presence of an unknown factor or modification that shields or stabilizes the laminin network from NTN4 binding.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the NTN4 overexpression experiments.

claim: The loss of the DM midline barrier may be caused in part by 'stretching' of the basement membrane as the notochord and endoderm become increasingly separated due to the elongation of the DM.
source: We consider that the loss of the DM midline barrier may be caused in part by 'stretching' of the basement membrane as the notochord and endoderm become increasingly separated due to the elongation of the DM (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations and is illustrated in Figure 3J.

claim: The turnover of stable basement membranes occurs on the scale of weeks, but the midline barrier appears to degrade over just 12–24 hr.
source: The turnover of stable basement membranes occurs on the scale of weeks (Trier et al., 1990; Decaris et al., 2014), but the midline barrier appears to degrade over just 12–24 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on basement membrane turnover and observations of midline degradation kinetics.

claim: Basement membrane destruction can occur over a large area, such as by secretion of matrix metalloproteinases in metastasizing cancer.
source: In other contexts, basement membrane destruction can occur over a large area, such as by secretion of matrix metalloproteinases in metastasizing cancer (Miyoshi et al., 2004; Miyoshi et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on basement membrane destruction in cancer.

claim: Basement membrane destruction can be more localized, as exhibited by invadopodia on immune or cancer cells before metastasis.
source: or more localized, as exhibited by invadopodia on immune or cancer cells before metastasis (Sekiguchi and Yamada, 2018; Santiago-Medina et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on invadopodia and basement membrane destruction.

claim: Localized basement membrane breakdown is seen in critical developmental processes, including mouth development in deuterostome embryos.
source: Such localized basement membrane breakdown is seen in critical developmental processes, including mouth development in deuterostome embryos (Dickinson and Sive, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on mouth development.

claim: The oral membrane includes a basement membrane that closes off the digestive system from the outside world, and this basement membrane specifically disintegrates to rupture that membrane to open the early mouth cavity.
source: The oral membrane includes a basement membrane that closes off the digestive system from the outside world. This basement membrane specifically disintegrates to rupture that membrane to open the early mouth cavity (Dickinson and Sive, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on oral membrane development.

claim: A basement membrane divides the two halves of the embryonic brain, and must be broken down at the site of the corpus callosum for neurons to cross for inter-hemisphere communication in the cerebrum.
source: In addition, a basement membrane divides the two halves of the embryonic brain, and must be broken down at the site of the corpus callosum for neurons to cross for inter-hemisphere communication in the cerebrum (Hakanen and Salminen, 2015; Gobius et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on brain development.

claim: Localized basement membrane dissolution is critical for optic cup fusion, where a contact-dependent dissolution of basement membrane occurs between the two sides of the optic fissure.
source: Localized basement membrane dissolution is also critical for optic cup fusion, where a contact-dependent dissolution of basement membrane occurs between the two sides of the optic fissure (Torres et al., 1996; Barbieri et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on optic cup fusion.

claim: Coloboma, a congenital eye defect where some tissue is missing inside the eye resulting in an enlarged, irregular pupil, occurs when optic fusion arrests.
source: Coloboma, a congenital eye defect where some tissue is missing inside the eye resulting in an enlarged, irregular pupil, occurs when optic fusion arrests (Patel and Sowden, 2019; ALSomiry et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on coloboma.

claim: In all examples of localized basement membrane breakdown and the case of the midline, the location of basement membrane breakdown is very specific—neighboring basement membranes appear unaffected.
source: It is worth noting that in all of these examples and the case of the midline, the location of basement membrane breakdown is very specific—neighboring basement membranes appear unaffected (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is an observation based on the data presented in Figure 3H and comparisons to other examples.

claim: Basement membrane breakdown in the DM may not simply be a passive process but may be required by the embryo for later events in gut development or vascular patterning.
source: Together, these findings support the idea that basement membrane breakdown in the DM may not simply be a passive process but may be required by the embryo for later events in gut development or vascular patterning.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observations and comparisons to other developmental processes.

claim: Signals produced from axial structures in the embryo are critical for the establishment of LR asymmetry.
source: It has long been known that signals produced from axial structures in the embryo are critical for the establishment of LR asymmetry, but it has been difficult for researchers to pin down which 'midline structure' or 'midline signal' is actually responsible.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The heart, lungs, and kidneys all rely on 'dorsal midline structures' to develop properly.
source: For example, the heart (Lohr et al., 1997; Chen et al., 1997), lungs (Arraf et al., 2016), and kidneys (James and Schultheiss, 2003) all rely on 'dorsal midline structures' to develop properly.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on organ development.

claim: 'Horseshoe kidney', in which the kidneys stay close to the midline and fuse at their posterior end, is an aberration from the loss of midline structures like the notochord.
source: Aberrations from the loss of midline structures like the notochord include 'horseshoe kidney', in which the kidneys stay close to the midline and fuse at their posterior end (Natsis et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on horseshoe kidney.

claim: Horseshoe kidney is due to the lack of notochordal Shh signaling.
source: This is due to the lack of notochordal Shh signaling, but the 'midline barrier' that exists downstream from this Shh signaling remains a mystery (Tripathi et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on Shh signaling and kidney development.

claim: The aorta begins as two parallel tubes with an avascular zone in between (where the midline is), but progressively they fuse into one with an anterior-to-posterior wave until the level of the vitelline arteries.
source: The aorta begins as two parallel tubes with an avascular zone in between (where the midline is) (Garriock et al., 2010), but progressively they fuse into one with an anterior-to-posterior wave until the level of the vitelline arteries (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Garriock et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on aortic fusion and is illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Fusion of the aortae coincides with the fragmentation and disappearance of the midline, suggesting that these two processes may be inextricably linked.
source: Fusion of the aortae coincides with the fragmentation and disappearance of the midline, suggesting that these two processes may be inextricably linked.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal correlation between aortic fusion and midline disappearance.

claim: Proper timing of aortic fusion depends on carefully balanced levels of VEGF, SHH, and the anterior-to-posterior wave of downregulation of the BMP-inhibitory genes Chordin and Noggin from the notochord.
source: Proper timing of this fusion depends on carefully balanced levels of VEGF (Jadon et al., 2023). SHH (Vokes et al., 2004), and the anterior-to-posterior wave of downregulation of the BMP-inhibitory genes Chordin and Noggin from the notochord (Garriock et al., 2010; Reese et al., 2004; Sato, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work on aortic fusion.

claim: There is evidence that VEGF signaling pulls VE-cadherin away from its cell-cell junctions, which may be important for the remodeling of the aortic endothelium during fusion and may be linked to the breaking of the DM midline barrier.
source: The precise mechanism of dorsal aorta fusion remains unknown, although there is evidence that VEGF signaling pulls VE-cadherin away from its cell-cell junctions (Jadon et al., 2023). This relocalization may be important for the remodeling of the aortic endothelium during fusion and may be linked to the breaking of the DM midline barrier.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on VEGF signaling and is a speculation about the link to midline breakdown.

claim: Microindentation analyses at HH21 show that the condensed left DM is significantly stiffer than the expanded right DM, and that proper gut tilting is dependent on this difference being tightly regulated.
source: Microindentation analyses at HH21 show that the condensed left DM is significantly stiffer than the expanded right DM, and that proper gut tilting is dependent on this difference being tightly regulated (Sanketi et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on DM stiffness.

claim: It is possible that the midline barrier helps to segregate the stiffness-influencing components of each side and provides a 'wall' for the right side to push upon in order to swing the gut tube toward the left.
source: It is possible that the midline barrier helps to segregate the stiffness-influencing components of each side (i.e. covalently modified HA on the right [Sivakumar et al., 2018], N-cadherin on the left [Kurpios et al., 2008]) and provides a 'wall' for the right side to push upon in order to swing the gut tube toward the left.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observations and prior work on DM stiffness and asymmetries.

claim: During the formation of gut arteries, a small subset of gut vascular endothelial cells migrate from right to left, closely adjacent to the dorsal tip of the endoderm, but they do not traverse the midline.
source: Likewise, during the formation of gut arteries, a small subset of gut vascular endothelial cells migrate from right to left, closely adjacent to the dorsal tip of the endoderm, but they do not traverse the midline (Mahadevan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on vascular endothelial cell migration.

claim: When the midline basement membrane is present and intact, N-cadherin expression is symmetric across the DM, but becomes asymmetric and left-specific upon midline disintegration.
source: Moreover, when the midline basement membrane is present and intact, N-cadherin expression is symmetric across the DM, but becomes asymmetric and left-specific upon midline disintegration (Kurpios et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on N-cadherin expression.

claim: While the midline is intact, the double basement membrane structure appears sufficient to segregate left and right cells, but when the midline disappears, a new cellular separation mechanism is required to maintain asymmetric compartments and N-cadherin functions in this role.
source: This may represent a shift in cell segregation mechanisms in the DM—while the midline is intact, the double basement membrane structure appears sufficient to segregate left and right cells. When the midline disappears, a new cellular separation mechanism is required to maintain asymmetric compartments and N-cadherin functions in this role.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observations of midline dynamics and N-cadherin expression.

claim: Looping patterns of the midgut are stereotypical between individuals but vary between species.
source: Looping patterns of the midgut are stereotypical between individuals but vary between species (Savin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on gut looping patterns.

claim: Differential growth rates between the gut tube and the DM have been identified as the primary means by which distinct gut looping patterns may be achieved.
source: While differential growth rates between the gut tube and the DM have been identified as the primary means by which distinct gut looping patterns may be achieved (Savin et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on gut looping mechanisms.

claim: It is possible that mesentery-specific changes such as modifications to the kinetics of asymmetry in the DM may impact looping patterns with potentially adaptive impact on diet and therefore niche utilization.
source: it is also possible that mesentery-specific changes such as modifications to the kinetics of asymmetry in the DM may impact looping patterns with potentially adaptive impact on diet and therefore niche utilization.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary implications of DM asymmetry kinetics.

claim: The presence, permeability, and timing of degradation of the midline basement membrane may provide evolution with an additional means of fine-tuning looping patterns between species.
source: The presence, permeability, and timing of degradation of the midline basement membrane may provide evolution with an additional means of fine-tuning looping patterns between species.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary implications of the midline basement membrane.

claim: Prior studies have observed midline laminin deposition in the mouse gut located between the separating notochord and endoderm, further suggesting conservation of a midline basement membrane in amniotes.
source: In mammals, prior studies have observed midline laminin deposition in the mouse gut located between the separating notochord and endoderm, further suggesting conservation of a midline basement membrane in amniotes (Li et al., 2007; Hajduk et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on mouse gut development.
